Catherine II. Known as Catherine the Great, she was the longest-reigning Russian empress and one of history's most effective autocrats. A German princess born Sophie of Anhalt-Zerbst, she married into the Romanov dynasty in 1745 as part of a diplomatic alliance. In 1762, she deposed her incompetent and unpopular husband Peter III in a bloodless coup, aided by Grigory Orlov and the imperial guard. She ruled as regent, then declared herself empress, drawing legitimacy from the love of the nobility and military rather than from inheritance alone.

Under her rule, Russia expanded to its greatest territorial extent. She conducted two Russo-Turkish Wars, between 1768 and 1774, and again between 1787 and 1792, annexing the Crimea, parts of the Caucasus, and gaining crucial access to the Black Sea. She partitioned Poland three times—in 1772, 1793, and 1795—with Prussia and Austria, absorbing vast Western territories and millions of Polish and Lithuanian subjects. She fought a brief conflict with Sweden between 1788 and 1790, securing control of the Baltic. She expanded the empire eastward into Siberia and southward to the borders of Ottoman Turkey and Persia.

Culturally and intellectually, she positioned herself as an enlightened monarch. She corresponded with Voltaire and Diderot, absorbing the intellectual currents of the Enlightenment. She established schools and legal codes based on Enlightenment principles. She patronized the arts, literature, and architecture, making St. Petersburg a center of European culture, rivaling Paris and Vienna. She created a meritocratic nobility through the Guberniia Reform in 1775, centralizing provincial administration.

Yet there was a profound contradiction at the heart of her reign. While she spoke the language of reason and progress, she refused to abolish serfdom, the institution of feudal servitude that bound peasants to the land. She consolidated nobility support through generous grants of land and serfs, binding the aristocracy to throne loyalty. When the massive peasant rebellion of Emelyan Pugachev erupted between 1773 and 1775, it terrified her. She responded by strengthening the institution of serfdom, binding peasants even more tightly to the land.

Catherine the Great represents enlightened absolutism at its apex: she wielded power with ruthless pragmatism while speaking the language of progress. She made Russia unambiguously European and unambiguously dominant in Eastern Europe. Yet her refusal to reform serfdom, despite her philosophical commitment to rational governance, ensured that modernization remained confined to the aristocracy and urban centers. This contradiction would split open a century later under her descendants, setting the stage for the revolutionary upheaval that would eventually consume the empire.
